subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.activity_title: Kitchen Observations: What Makes Things Work?
periods.textbook_anchor: What is Energy? — Students observe a kitchen scene and discuss what makes things move, shine, make a sound, or get warm and cold (p. 115)

time_bands.activity: Students close their eyes and recall their home kitchen in the morning. The teacher asks: What do you see happening? What do you hear? What do you feel? Students share observations aloud in pairs before opening to Textbook p. 115.

Students open Textbook p. 115 and study the kitchen scene. In small groups they list every action happening — something moving, glowing, making a sound, getting warm. Groups share their lists and the teacher collects responses on the board under four columns: Move | Shine | Sound | Warm.

The class discusses the Textbook p. 115 question: What makes these things move, shine, make a sound, or get warm and cold? Students suggest ideas freely. The teacher draws out the word 'energy' from student language without defining it formally, letting the class build a working description together.

Each student writes two sentences in their notebook: one naming an action from the kitchen picture, and one answering what they think makes that action happen. The teacher invites two or three students to read their sentences aloud to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify observable actions in an everyday environment and connect each action to the idea that something must supply the push or pull that causes it.
periods.section_context: Kitchen scene activities — cooking, movement, light, sound, warmth; teacher question on what makes things move, shine, make a sound, or get warm and cold.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'When you switch on a torch, where does the light come from — does it come from nothing?' Use this to nudge students toward the idea that energy is always transferred from somewhere, without introducing technical vocabulary yet.

periods.textbook_anchor: What is Energy? — Students inflate a balloon, release it, and observe what happens (p. 116)

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds an uninflated balloon and asks: What do I have to do to make this balloon move without touching it after I let go? Students predict in one sentence what will happen when the mouth is released.

Students work in pairs following Textbook p. 116. One student blows the balloon full; the partner holds it tightly. On a count, the mouth is released. Both students watch carefully and then answer in their notebooks: What happened? Which direction did the balloon go? What did you feel or hear?

Class discussion: What made the balloon move? Students share observations. The teacher introduces the phrase 'stored energy becoming movement energy' using student language, and writes 'kinetic energy' on the board as the name for movement energy. The class connects this to their kitchen list from the previous discussion — which items there showed movement?

Students sketch the balloon experiment in their notebook — before and after release — and label where the energy was stored and where it went. They write one sentence explaining what kinetic energy means in their own words.
Quick whole-class share: teacher asks one student to read their sentence. The class gives a thumbs-up if they agree.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a simple release-and-observe investigation and use the observation to describe how stored energy converts to movement.
periods.section_context: Balloon inflated and released; observation of movement, direction, and sound; kinetic energy from stored air pressure.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students struggle to connect stored air to stored energy, ask: 'What did you have to do to put energy into the balloon — was it easy or did it take effort?' This connects muscular effort to energy input.

periods.activity_title: Rubber Band Guitar: Making Sound Energy
periods.textbook_anchor: What is Energy? — Students release a balloon and observe what happens (p. 116)
materials: Rubber bands of two or three different thicknesses
Empty open box or plastic container (one per group)

time_bands.activity: Teacher stretches a rubber band and asks: What happens when I pluck it? Students predict aloud. Teacher plucks it and the class listens. Question: Where did this sound come from? What did I do to create it?

Groups of four stretch rubber bands of different thicknesses across their open box to make a simple guitar. Each group plucks each band, listens carefully, and records in a quick table: thick / thin / tightly stretched / loosely stretched — and whether the sound is high, low, loud, or soft. Groups try plucking gently and plucking hard to compare.

Each group shares one finding. The class builds a shared conclusion: plucking (movement) creates vibration, vibration creates sound — movement energy becomes sound energy. Teacher writes 'sound energy' on the board alongside 'kinetic energy' from the balloon unit.

Students write in their notebooks: two observations from the rubber band guitar and one sentence connecting movement to sound using the word 'energy'. They also add 'sound energy' to their earlier kitchen observation list next to any kitchen item that made sound.
Teacher asks: 'Can you name one more place where movement creates sound?' Students call out answers.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe that mechanical action on an object produces sound, and describe this as a form of energy conversion.
periods.section_context: Rubber band guitar; thick and thin rubber bands across an open box; plucking to produce sound; variation in pitch and volume with thickness and tension.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'What happens to the rubber band while it is making sound — is it still or moving?' Drawing attention to the vibration connects movement and sound without the teacher stating it first.

periods.activity_title: Sun-Powered Water Warmer: Heat from the Sun
periods.textbook_anchor: What is Energy? — Students inflate a balloon, release it, and observe what happens (p. 116)
materials: Thermometer (if available) or fingers to test warmth
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 116 sun-powered water warmer illustration

time_bands.activity: Teacher places two cups of water — one wrapped in black paper, one in white — in direct sunlight before students arrive, or sets them up now at a sunny window. Students observe both cups and predict which will feel warmer after the unit, recording their prediction in their notebook.

While cups warm, students open Textbook p. 116 and study the sun-powered water warmer illustration. In pairs they answer: What is the energy source? What kind of energy does the sun provide? What change does it cause in the water? They discuss with their partner and write two sentences.

Students touch both cups carefully (or use a thermometer) and record their observations: which is warmer, by how much (warmer / much warmer / same), and whether the prediction was correct. The class pools observations on the board.

Discussion: Why did the black-wrapped cup feel warmer? Where did the heat come from? Students connect this to 'heat energy' from the Sun. Teacher adds 'heat energy' to the board list. Students also discuss: Do we use this idea at home or in our area — dark surfaces, solar water heaters, anything similar?
Students add 'heat energy' to their notebook energy list and write one sentence: 'The Sun gives us _______ energy, which can _______.' They fill both blanks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and observe a simple colour-absorption comparison and use the result to describe how sunlight transfers heat energy to objects.
periods.section_context: Sun-powered water warmer; black-covered and white-covered cups in sunlight; observation of heat absorbed; heat energy from the Sun.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone at home have a black water tank on the roof? Have you noticed whether that water is warmer?' This draws out local experience of solar heat without naming it as a formal concept.

periods.activity_title: Fuels and Fires: The Diya Investigation
periods.textbook_anchor: Sources of Energy — Students place cotton wicks with and without oil in two diyas, light them, and observe which burns longer and what is acting as fuel (p. 120)
materials: Two small diyas or clay lamps

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a question: If food is energy for our bodies, what is energy for a lamp? Students discuss in pairs and share ideas. Teacher introduces the word 'fuel' and writes it on the board. Students open Textbook p. 120 and read the setup for the diya activity.

Teacher (or a designated adult) sets up two diyas at the front: Diya 1 with a dry cotton wick, Diya 2 with a wick soaked in oil. Students observe the setup and record in their notebook before lighting: Prediction — Which will burn longer and why? Teacher lights both diyas under strict safety supervision. Students watch carefully and record what they see.

Students answer the Textbook p. 120 questions in their notebooks: Which diya burns longer? Why? What is acting as fuel here? Class discussion pools answers. Teacher draws out the idea that oil is the fuel — it stores energy that is released as light and heat when it burns.

Discussion extends to fuels at home: cooking gas, wood, coal, petrol, diesel. Students answer Textbook p. 120 discuss questions — what fuel is used at home, and what problems come from using too much wood or coal. Teacher introduces the idea that burning some fuels creates pollution. Students who know of traditional practices — diyas at festivals, wood fires in certain regions — share those connections.
Students write one sentence: 'A fuel is ________ because it _________.' Two students share their sentences aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a controlled comparison of two conditions and use the result to identify what property makes a substance a fuel.
periods.section_context: Diya 1 with dry cotton wick; Diya 2 with cotton wick and oil; observation of burn duration; oil as fuel; cooking gas, wood, coal, petrol, diesel as fuel types; pollution from burning wood or coal.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen a diya lit at home for a festival or puja? How long did it burn — what kept it going?' This naturally surfaces the cultural use of diyas without labelling it as a special category.

periods.activity_title: Cattle, Cold Climates, and Energy Choices
periods.textbook_anchor: Sources of Energy — How is food cooked in your house? (p. 119)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 119 illustration of cooking methods

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 119 and answer the Write task individually: How is food cooked in your house? They write two to three sentences. The teacher collects a quick show of hands: gas stove, wood fire, electric stove, other. Results are tallied on the board.

Discussion: Why do families in different places use different fuels? Teacher presents the story from the textbook — in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Ladakh, families traditionally keep cattle on the ground floor of their home so the animals' body heat rises and warms the family living above, reducing the need for firewood in freezing winters. Teacher asks: What problem does this solve? Where does the heat energy come from? Is this a smart use of energy?

Students compare: the diya used oil as fuel; the cattle practice uses body heat. Both are ways of getting energy from a source. In pairs, students discuss: What other creative ways have families or communities found to get warmth or light without extra fuel? Students share ideas — thick-walled houses, courtyards, south-facing windows. Teacher notes all responses without judging them.

Students write in their notebook: two facts about fuels and one sentence about how one community uses a natural energy source cleverly. They may draw a simple diagram of the two-storey cattle-and-family house if they wish.
Teacher closes with: 'Every energy choice has a reason behind it — geography, climate, or what is available. We will keep this idea in mind as we explore more sources.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how communities choose energy sources based on geography and climate, and describe one traditional practice that uses a natural energy source without burning fuel.
periods.section_context: Cooking methods at home; gas stove, wood fire, electric stove; cattle kept on ground floor for body-heat warmth (Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Ladakh); body heat as energy source; comparison of fuel use across contexts.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Could you imagine doing this in our town or region? Why or why not?' This keeps the discussion geographically grounded and invites students to think about why different solutions emerge in different climates.

periods.activity_title: Electricity at Home: Device Survey and Safety Rules
periods.textbook_anchor: Electricity — Students walk around home or classroom, identify five electrical devices, and fill in a table of device, what it does, and what it requires (p. 121)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: What would our classroom look like right now if there were no electricity at all? Students visualise and share. Teacher then says: Let us find out how much electricity we actually use without realising it.

Students open Textbook p. 121 and carry out the observation walk around the classroom. Each student identifies five electrical devices and fills in the table from Textbook p. 121: Device | What it does | What it requires (light / sound / heat / movement / cooling / other). Students work individually and quietly so they can observe carefully.

Class pools findings on the board. Teacher organises the list into columns: Light | Sound | Heat | Movement | Cooling. Students check whether their table matches the class list. Discussion: Is there anything on our list that does more than one thing — like a TV that gives both light and sound?

Teacher reads the safety rules from the textbook section — not touching wires, avoiding sockets, staying away from fallen poles and transformers. For each rule, students suggest: What could go wrong if we broke this rule? Teacher also introduces LED bulbs and traditional thick-walled houses as examples of using energy efficiently — the same job, less energy used.
Students write one safety rule in their notebook and explain it in their own words. One student shares with the class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically identify electrical devices in their immediate environment, classify what each device does, and state the safety rules for using electricity.
periods.section_context: Five electrical devices in classroom or home; table of device, what it does, what it requires; light, sound, heat, movement, cooling; LED bulbs as energy-efficient; safety rules for electricity; traditional thick-walled houses as passive energy design.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which device on our list do you think uses the most electricity — and how could you find out?' This opens a line of reasoning about energy efficiency that connects naturally to the LED bulb example.

periods.activity_title: Build a Pinwheel: Wind Energy in Action
periods.section_ref: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
periods.textbook_anchor: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water — Students make a paper pinwheel and observe it spin in wind (p. 123)
materials: Square piece of paper (one per student)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: Has anyone seen a windmill — in a field, a picture, or a toy? What was it doing? Students share. Teacher connects: today we will build a tiny windmill and test what wind can do.

Students open Textbook p. 123 and follow the step-by-step instructions to build their pinwheel: draw two diagonals on a square paper, cut halfway along each line, fold every alternate corner to the centre, and pin to a stick. Teacher circulates and helps with folding and pinning. Students should complete the construction before testing.

Students take their pinwheels to a window or doorway and hold them in any available wind. If no wind is available, they walk briskly holding the pinwheel up. They observe and answer in their notebook: What made the pinwheel spin? What would happen if the wind stopped? How could we make the pinwheel spin faster?

Class discussion: Where do we see wind energy used on a large scale? Teacher introduces windmills, wind turbines, and the ancient Indian maritime trade — merchants from Gujarat and Tamil Nadu who used wind-powered sails on ships. Students note in their book: two real-world uses of wind energy.
Teacher asks: 'Is wind a fuel? Why or why not?' Students give a quick oral answer.

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct a simple wind-driven device, test it under different wind conditions, and use the result to describe how moving air transfers energy.
periods.section_context: Paper pinwheel construction; diagonals, cutting, folding, pinning; spinning in wind or while running; windmills; wind turbines; ancient maritime wind-powered sails (Gujarat, Tamil Nadu).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you made the pinwheel blades wider or longer, do you think it would spin faster or slower — and how could you test that?' This pushes students toward a simple variable-testing mindset.

periods.activity_title: Sunlight in Focus: Solar Heat Energy
periods.section_ref: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
periods.textbook_anchor: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water — Students use a magnifying glass to focus sunlight on paper and observe what happens (p. 124)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 124 magnifying glass activity illustration

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: Can sunlight alone cause a change in a material — without any fuel, no fire, no electricity? Students predict yes or no and give a reason. Teacher notes predictions on the board before the activity.

In groups of three, students open Textbook p. 124 and carry out the activity: place a piece of paper in direct sunlight and use the magnifying glass to focus the sunlight onto one spot on the paper. Students observe carefully what happens to that spot over time. Teacher supervises closely and ensures safety — students stop immediately if they see any scorching and move the glass away.

Groups share observations. The class builds a description: the magnifying glass concentrates sunlight into a small, intense point. This focused heat is enough to cause a change in the paper. Teacher connects this to solar panels and solar cookers — both concentrate or collect solar energy to do useful work.

Students write in their notebook: What happened to the paper? What did the magnifying glass do to the sunlight? Name one device that works on a similar idea. They also note the Cochin International Airport fact from the textbook — the world's first airport fully powered by solar energy — and write one sentence on why this matters.
Teacher closes: 'We used no fuel, no fire — just sunlight and a glass. What does this tell us about the Sun as an energy source?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can focus sunlight using a lens, observe the thermal effect, and relate this to how solar energy is harnessed for practical use.
periods.section_context: Magnifying glass focusing sunlight on paper; observation of heat effect; solar panels; solar cookers; Cochin International Airport powered by solar energy.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do we use a magnifying glass and not just let sunlight fall on the paper directly — what does the glass do that plain sunlight cannot?' This targets the concept of concentration of energy.

periods.activity_title: Paper-Cup Water Wheel: Energy from Flowing Water
periods.section_ref: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
periods.textbook_anchor: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water — Students build a paper-cup water wheel and pour water to observe whether it moves (p. 124)
materials: Container (bowl or tray) to catch water
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 124 water wheel construction diagram

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: A river flows constantly. Can that flowing water do work without any electricity or fuel? Students predict and share ideas.

Groups follow Textbook p. 124: make five holes evenly spaced around a paper cup, insert a plastic spoon in each hole, and push a pencil or straw through the base to serve as an axle. Balance the axle across a container. Students observe the wheel at rest, then pour water from the jug steadily onto the spoon blades and watch what happens.

Students record in their notebook: Did the water make the wheel move? What happened when more water was poured? What happened when less was poured? One student from each group reports one observation. The class agrees on a shared conclusion: moving water carries energy that can turn a wheel.

Teacher introduces gharaats — traditional watermills in hilly areas of India that use flowing streams to grind grain — as an example of this same principle used for centuries. Students discuss: How is a gharaat similar to our paper-cup wheel? What does the wheel's turning do in a real watermill? Teacher also mentions hydroelectric dams and fast-moving rivers as modern-scale uses of the same idea.
Students write: 'Flowing water has _______ energy. A gharaat uses this to _______.' Two students share their completed sentences.

periods.implied_lo: Students can build a water-driven wheel model, test it with varying water flow, and use the result to explain how moving water transfers energy to do mechanical work.
periods.section_context: Paper-cup water wheel; five spoons as blades; pencil as axle; water poured onto wheel; wheel rotation; gharaats (traditional watermills in hilly areas); hydroelectric dams; fast-moving rivers and waterfalls.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If we poured the water from higher up versus lower down onto the wheel, would it make a difference? Why?' This introduces the idea that the speed and height of falling water affects how much energy it has.

periods.activity_title: Energy Flow Game: Source → Type → Use
periods.section_ref: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
periods.textbook_anchor: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water — Energy Flow Game with paper slips of energy sources, types, and uses; students match and present their energy chain (p. 128)
materials: Pre-cut paper slips labelled: Sun, wind, water, food, fuel, electricity (sources); heat, light, movement, sound (types); drying clothes, lighting a bulb, turning a turbine, cooking, running (uses)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 127 energy flow picture / table

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes one slip to each student at random. Students read their slip silently and think: Am I a source, a type of energy, or a use? They do not share yet. Teacher opens Textbook p. 127 and students note the picture and table as reference.

Students walk around the class following Textbook p. 128 instructions — they are looking for two others who complete their energy chain: Source → Type → Use. When a group of three believes they have a complete chain, they stand together. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Can you explain how your source leads to your type? And how your type leads to your use?'

Each group presents their chain to the class in one sentence: 'The Sun gives us heat energy, which we use to dry clothes.' Class validates each chain — is the source real? Is the type correct? Does the use match? Any chain the class questions is discussed together and corrected if needed.

Students open Textbook p. 127 and complete the Write task: list actions from the picture and fill in the Activity and Source of Energy table. They also write one chain of their own that was not used in the game.
Teacher asks: 'Can you think of a chain where the same source produces two different types of energy at once?' Students call out answers to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace a complete energy chain from source through type to use, and justify each link in the chain with a reason.
periods.section_context: Energy Flow Game paper slips; sources: Sun, wind, water, food, fuel, electricity; types: heat, light, movement, sound; uses: drying clothes, lighting a bulb, turning a turbine, cooking, running; Textbook p. 127 activity-and-source table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups who are stuck: 'What does your source actually do to things around it — does it warm them, move them, light them up, or make them grow?' This helps students identify the energy type without you naming it for them.

periods.activity_title: Clean Energy Home Plan: Drawing and Reflection
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students draw or make a simple plan of a clean energy home using solar, wind, or similar sources (p. 130)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 130 and read silently the three reflection questions: What will happen if there is no electricity for a day? Why is solar or wind energy better than coal? What is one thing you can do at home to save energy? Students jot one-sentence answers to each question in their notebook before drawing.

Students follow the Textbook p. 130 Draw task: they plan and draw a simple 'clean energy home' that uses solar, wind, or another clean source. They label each energy source and what it powers. Students who finish early add a second energy source or label which room benefits from each source.

Gallery walk: students place their drawings on their desk and walk around to look at three classmates' plans. They leave a sticky note or whisper one compliment and one question to each. After the walk, each student returns to their seat and adds one improvement to their own drawing based on what they saw.
Teacher invites two students to explain their clean energy home plan in two sentences. Class listens and suggests one additional clean feature each plan could include.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design a simple plan that applies knowledge of clean energy sources to a real-world context, and justify their choices in words or labels.
periods.section_context: Clean energy home drawing; solar, wind, and other clean energy sources; labelling of energy source and what it powers; reflection questions on no-electricity day, solar versus coal, and personal energy-saving action.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If your home were in a very sunny place, which source would you choose most — and would your answer change if you lived on a windy coast or near a river?' This grounds the design task in geography without restricting what students draw.

periods.activity_title: Energy All Around Us: Whole-Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — What is the one thing you can do at home to save energy? (p. 130)
periods.visual_aids: Chalkboard diagram summarising energy forms and sources discussed across the chapter

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple web on the board: 'ENERGY' at the centre, with spokes for Sources, Forms, Uses, Conservation. Students call out every term, idea, or example they can remember from the chapter — balloon, rubber band, diya, wind, gharaat, LED, solar panels, cattle warmth — and teacher maps each to the right spoke. Nothing is judged; everything offered is placed somewhere.

Students open Textbook p. 130 and work through two reflection tasks in writing: first, they give two examples of stored energy they have seen; second, they list three objects around them with their energy source (the Textbook p. 130 List task). They connect every example they write to one of the chapter's energy forms — heat, light, movement, or sound — and write that form next to each example.

Discussion: the teacher poses a genuine dilemma — 'A family in a cold mountain village wants to keep warm through winter. They have access to firewood, animal heat from their cattle, and some hours of sunlight. What would you advise them to do, and why?' Students discuss in pairs, then share with the class. Teacher draws out trade-offs: pollution, availability, cost, tradition. The traditional cattle-warmth practice and solar options are both treated as valid answers depending on context.

Each student writes their personal energy commitment in their notebook: one thing they will do differently at home to save energy, and why it matters. Students who wish to share read their commitment aloud. Teacher names the value: caring for shared resources is something every person can practise, and small actions add up.

Teacher closes without summarising: 'Energy is everywhere — in the food you ate this morning, the light coming through the window, and the movement of your pencil just now. The question we carry forward is not just what energy is, but how we use it and whether we use it well.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect energy forms, sources, and uses across multiple real-world contexts, evaluate trade-offs in energy choices, and articulate a personal conservation commitment.
periods.section_context: Whole-chapter synthesis: balloon kinetic energy, rubber band sound energy, sun heat energy, diya as fuel, cattle body-heat warmth, cooking fuels and pollution, electrical devices and safety, pinwheel wind energy, magnifying-glass solar heat, water wheel and gharaats, energy flow chains, clean energy home; stored energy examples; personal energy-saving action.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which energy source discussed in this chapter surprised you most — and why does that surprise matter?' This opens reflective thinking rather than recall, and honours the range of traditional and modern examples students have encountered.

assessment_items.question_text: You are looking at a kitchen in the morning. The fan is spinning, the bulb is glowing, and something is cooking on the stove. What is the ONE thing that makes all three of these things happen?

options.label: A
options.text: Air

options.label: B
options.text: Energy

options.label: C
options.text: Sound

options.label: D
options.text: Water

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests whether students can name the common cause behind diverse kitchen phenomena observed in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify observable actions in an everyday environment and connect each action to the idea that something must supply the push or pull that causes it.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing Air shows the student may be thinking only of the fan and has not connected glowing and cooking to a common cause — a single-example confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing Water shows the student may associate cooking with water boiling, not recognising that water is an ingredient, not the cause of all three actions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing Sound shows the student may have fixated on the idea that kitchens are noisy, not that sound is itself produced by an energy supply.

assessment_items.question_text: When you blow air into a balloon and then let it go, the balloon shoots across the room. Where was the energy before you released the balloon? What form of energy did it become after you released it? Give one piece of evidence from the activity to support your answer.
expected_elements: States that energy was stored in the stretched balloon or compressed air before release.
Names kinetic energy (or movement energy) as the form it became after release.
Provides one observation as evidence — e.g., the balloon moved, flew across the room, or made a sound when released.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for all three elements. Partial credit if two elements are present. Accept 'movement energy' in place of 'kinetic energy' as the terminology is being introduced at this stage.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a simple release-and-observe investigation and use the observation to describe how stored energy converts to movement.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

assessment_items.question_text: When you pluck a stretched rubber band, it makes a sound. Which of the following best explains why?

options.label: A
options.text: The box underneath the rubber band makes the sound, not the rubber band itself.

options.label: B
options.text: The plucking movement makes the rubber band vibrate, and this vibration creates sound.

options.label: C
options.text: The rubber band absorbs light energy from the room and converts it to sound.

options.label: D
options.text: The rubber band becomes warm and releases heat, which we hear as sound.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item checks whether students can link the mechanical action of plucking to vibration to sound, the core energy conversion observed in the rubber band guitar activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe that mechanical action on an object produces sound, and describe this as a form of energy conversion.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing A shows a confusion between heat energy and sound energy — the student may remember that rubber can get warm when stretched but has not connected plucking to vibration.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing C shows a misconception that light is the source of sound, perhaps from general exposure to the idea that energy can be converted without understanding how.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing D shows the student may have noticed the box amplified the sound during the activity and incorrectly concluded the box, not the rubber band, was the source.

assessment_items.question_text: Two cups of water were placed in sunlight — one wrapped in black paper and one wrapped in white paper. After some time, the cup with black paper felt warmer. Why did this happen? What does this tell you about how the Sun gives us energy?
expected_elements: States that the black surface absorbs more sunlight (or more heat) than the white surface.
Explains that the absorbed sunlight transferred heat energy to the water in the black-covered cup.
Draws a general conclusion that the Sun provides heat energy that can be absorbed by objects.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for all three elements. Accept 'the black paper soaks up more sun' as equivalent to the absorption concept at this stage.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and observe a simple colour-absorption comparison and use the result to describe how sunlight transfers heat energy to objects.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: States that the black surface absorbs more sunlight (or more heat) than the white surface.
Explains that the absorbed sunlight transferred heat energy to the water in the black-covered cup.
Draws a general conclusion that the Sun provides heat energy that can be absorbed by objects.

assessment_items.question_text: Two diyas are set up: Diya 1 has a dry cotton wick with no oil, and Diya 2 has a cotton wick with oil. Both are lit at the same time. Which diya burns longer, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Both burn for the same time because both have the same cotton wick.

options.label: B
options.text: Diya 1, because the dry wick burns faster and brighter.

options.label: C
options.text: Diya 2, because the oil acts as a fuel that keeps supplying energy to the flame.

options.label: D
options.text: Diya 2, because the oil keeps the wick wet and prevents it from catching fire.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item checks whether students understood that oil is the fuel — the energy supplier — not just a liquid that coats the wick.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a controlled comparison of two conditions and use the result to identify what property makes a substance a fuel.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing A shows the student may have a misconception that dryness helps combustion — they have not connected the concept of fuel as an energy store to how long the flame lasts.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing C shows the student recognised the shared wick but missed the key variable — the oil — suggesting they did not correctly isolate what changed between the two diyas.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing D shows the student correctly identified that Diya 2 burns longer but gave a wrong reason — confusing oil as a coolant or protective coating rather than as a fuel.

assessment_items.question_text: In some parts of India — such as Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Ladakh — families traditionally keep their cattle on the ground floor of their home during cold winters, while the family lives on the floor above. Why do you think this was done? Do you think this is a smart way to use energy? Give reasons for your answer.
look_for: Identifies that cattle produce body heat, which rises and warms the floor above — connecting animal biology to heat energy.
Recognises that this practice reduces or replaces the need for firewood or other fuels in a cold climate.
Evaluates the practice with a reason — e.g., it is smart because it uses a naturally available source without burning anything, or it has limits such as the smell or space required.
Shows awareness that geography (cold climate, mountain region) shapes this energy choice.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response names body heat as the energy source, explains the climate reason, and gives a reasoned evaluation. Partial credit if the student explains the mechanism but does not evaluate, or evaluates without explaining the heat transfer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how communities choose energy sources based on geography and climate, and describe one traditional practice that uses a natural energy source without burning fuel.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

assessment_items.question_text: A student surveys her classroom and finds: a ceiling fan, a tube light, an electric bell, and a computer. She is making a table with columns for 'what the device does'. Which row is CORRECTLY filled?

options.label: A
options.text: Ceiling fan → gives heat

options.label: B
options.text: Computer → gives cooling

options.label: C
options.text: Electric bell → gives sound

options.label: D
options.text: Tube light → gives movement

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The item checks whether students can classify what an electrical device does — the core task of the observation survey. Note: a computer can give light, sound, and movement, but not primarily cooling; the distractor tests that specific confusion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically identify electrical devices in their immediate environment, classify what each device does, and state the safety rules for using electricity.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing A shows the student may be confusing the fan's motor warmth with its purpose — they have not distinguished what a device produces as its main output from the heat all motors generate.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing B shows the student may be thinking of the physical act of switching the light on as 'movement' — a confusion between operating the device and what the device produces.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing D shows the student may be conflating a computer with an air conditioner or refrigerator — devices that primarily produce cooling — suggesting imprecise classification of electrical devices.

assessment_items.question_text: You built a paper pinwheel and held it in the wind — it spun. Then you held it still in a room with no wind — it stopped. What does this tell you about what wind can do? Name one real machine or object that uses this same idea on a large scale.
expected_elements: States that moving air (wind) carries energy that can make things spin or move.
Explains that without wind (moving air), the energy is not available and the pinwheel stops.
Names a real-world example that uses wind energy — e.g., a windmill, wind turbine, or sailing ship.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for all three elements. Accept 'wind turbine', 'windmill', 'sailing boat', or 'ship with sails' as valid real-world examples. Regional examples such as traditional wind-powered fishing boats are also acceptable.

assessment_items.question_text: A student held a magnifying glass over a piece of white paper in direct sunlight. After a short time, a dark spot appeared on the paper where the glass was focused. What was the magnifying glass doing to the sunlight? How does this idea help us in real life — give one example.
expected_elements: Explains that the magnifying glass concentrates (focuses) sunlight onto a small spot, making it much more intense.
States that the concentrated sunlight has enough heat energy to cause a visible change in the paper.
Gives one real-life example of using concentrated solar energy — e.g., a solar cooker, solar panels, or the Cochin Airport powered by solar energy.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for all three elements. 'Focuses' or 'concentrates' both accepted for the first element. Any example of practical solar use is valid for the third element.

assessment_items.question_text: You built a paper-cup water wheel and poured water over it — the wheel turned. How is this similar to how a gharaat works? What kind of energy does the flowing water have, and what does the wheel do with it?
expected_elements: States that flowing water has movement energy (kinetic energy) that pushes the blades and makes the wheel turn.
Explains that a gharaat works on the same principle — flowing stream water turns a wheel that grinds grain.
Identifies the energy conversion: the movement energy of water becomes the mechanical work of turning the wheel.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for all three elements. Accept 'watermill' as equivalent to 'gharaat'. Accept 'movement energy' or 'kinetic energy' for the energy type.

assessment_items.question_text: In the Energy Flow Game, a student holds the card 'the Sun'. Which complete chain is CORRECT for this card?

options.label: A
options.text: The Sun → electricity → cooking gas

options.label: B
options.text: The Sun → heat → drying clothes

options.label: C
options.text: The Sun → movement → turning a turbine

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun → sound → ringing a bell

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The item checks whether students can correctly link the Sun as a source to heat as an energy type and then to a matching use, as practised in the Energy Flow Game.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace a complete energy chain from source through type to use, and justify each link in the chain with a reason.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing A shows the student has not connected the Sun to heat energy — they may know 'sound' as an energy type from earlier activities but have not sorted it to a source correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing B shows partial understanding — the Sun can eventually drive turbines via solar power, but the direct energy type from the Sun is heat, not movement. The student has skipped a step in the chain.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing D shows a confusion between electricity (which the Sun can ultimately generate via solar panels) and cooking gas (a fossil fuel) — the student has not recognised that cooking gas is a separate fuel source, not a use of solar energy.

assessment_items.task: Draw a simple plan of a home that runs on clean energy. Label at least two different energy sources you have chosen and draw an arrow from each source to what it powers in the home. Below your drawing, write two sentences: one explaining why you chose these sources, and one describing one thing the family in your home could do to use even less energy.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about the sources of clean energy explored in this chapter — the Sun, the wind, and flowing water. Which would work best for a home in your region? Draw the home, show where the energy comes from, and label what each source powers. Then write your two sentences.
format_of_output: Labelled drawing of a home with at least two clean energy sources
Arrows connecting each source to what it powers
Two written sentences — one justifying the choice of sources, one suggesting an energy-saving action
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation applies: students may name solar, wind, or water sources depending on their local geography. A student in a coastal area naming wind energy and one in a sunny plain naming solar are both correct. Accept any clean energy source discussed in the chapter. Assess the justification for coherence, not for a specific 'right' source.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design a simple plan that applies knowledge of clean energy sources to a real-world context, and justify their choices in words or labels.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can apply knowledge of clean energy sources to a self-designed real-world scenario, and whether they can articulate a reasoned justification for their choices and a conservation action.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold asks students to recall the three clean sources, select based on their region, and express their reasoning in both image and text. A student who draws but does not label, or labels but does not write sentences, has partially met the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response labels two distinct clean sources with arrows to specific uses (e.g., solar panels → lights; windmill → fan), gives a geographically grounded justification, and names a concrete conservation action. A weak response draws a house with a sun symbol but no labels or arrows, and leaves sentences vague ('use less electricity').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write both sentences may draw a third energy source with a label instead. Students who cannot draw may describe their home plan in words. Both alternatives demonstrate the same underlying competency.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing externalises spatial reasoning about energy systems; the sentences require the student to articulate their reasoning — together they test both application and evaluation at this stage.

assessment_items.task: A family in a cold mountain village wants to stay warm through winter. They have access to firewood, the body heat of their cattle, and some hours of sunlight each day. Write a letter to this family advising them on the best way to use these energy sources. In your letter: (a) explain what energy each source gives them, (b) advise which sources are better for the environment and why, and (c) suggest one action they can take to save energy.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about all the sources of energy you have explored in this chapter — fuels, body heat, and sunlight. Each one gives a different kind of energy. Some create pollution; some do not. Use what you know to give clear, helpful advice to the family. Your letter should have a greeting, three pieces of advice, and a closing.
format_of_output: A letter with a greeting and closing
Explanation of the energy each source provides
Reasoned recommendation of the more environmentally sound option(s)
assessment_items.annotation: This synthesis item draws on content from across the chapter — fuels and pollution (Sources of Energy), cattle body heat (Sources of Energy), and solar energy (Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water). Accept any reasoned argument that correctly identifies burning firewood as polluting and body heat or sunlight as cleaner alternatives. Regional variation in the energy-saving suggestion is acceptable and expected.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect energy forms, sources, and uses across multiple real-world contexts, evaluate trade-offs in energy choices, and articulate a personal conservation commitment.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can synthesise knowledge of multiple energy sources, evaluate them on environmental grounds, and communicate a reasoned recommendation — drawing on content from across the whole chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to address all three required elements in a letter format. A student who advises correctly but uses no letter format has still demonstrated the core competency; format should not be the primary basis for evaluation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response correctly names what energy each source provides (firewood → heat but polluting; cattle → body heat; sunlight → solar heat), clearly recommends the cleaner options with a reason, and gives a specific actionable saving suggestion. A weak response lists the sources but does not evaluate them or gives a suggestion ('use less') that lacks any reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find letter writing challenging may present their advice as a numbered list instead. Students may also draw a diagram comparing the three sources if they prefer a visual response, provided they add at least two written labels explaining their reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The letter format requires students to address a real audience with a real problem, which pushes beyond recall into genuine evaluation and communication — the culminating skill of the synthesis unit.
